extracted.intended_audience: historians of advertising, journalists, and general readers interested in 18th-century newspaper and advertising history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and comments on late-18th-century newspaper practice and advertising tactics, with examples from The Times and contemporary adverts. Useful for understanding how newspapers gathered news and how adverts were worded to persuade specific audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / being first
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the ever-present desire to be first wherever possible' — the Times announced the capitulation of Flushing two days before the news reached other channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being first is shown as an explicit aim: use superior activity and stratagem, despatch well-qualified reporters, and cultivate early intelligence to outpace official or ministerial channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and integrity in journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: 'its present eminence is due to nothing but perseverance and integrity' (on The Times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial persistence and refusal to accept improper favours (e.g., rejecting conditional access from government) are presented as core virtues, even at the cost of fines or imprisonment; these principles underpin long-term reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fullness and accuracy of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The debates in Parliament, law proceedings, public meetings, and commercial affairs, were all reported with a fulness and accuracy which filled readers with wonder.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports should aim for comprehensive and accurate accounts of public events (debates, trials, meetings, commercial news) to inform and satisfy readers; completeness is a quality metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing: employ and retain the best writers, correspondents and reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The best writers were employed... Correspondents were posted in every great city in the world, and well-qualified reporters were despatched to every scene of public interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in talented writers and a global correspondent/reporting network; identify and 'look after' high-ability individuals so their skills are utilised — staffing quality directly affects newspaper caliber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-page / headline design to attract readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages arise from 'placing a taking title-page before a book, or an inviting Head on the front page of a NEWs-pAPea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-chosen, striking head or title-page functions as an attention-capture device for passers-by; newspaper heads are compared to theatrical or book title-pages as tools to draw readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secrecy and honour as an advertising tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Strict honour and secrecy seems to be an essential to the successful completion of the designs of many advertisers of this time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adverts offering sensitive services (e.g., confidential retirement/accommodation for a lady, lottery systems, procuring matches or positions) explicitly promise secrecy and honour to persuade respondents and protect reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target adverts to social class and genteel sensibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverts describe desired respondents as 'genteel', 'having a liberal Education', 'some independance of her own', and emphasize genteel style and respectability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use class markers, references to education, independence, and genteel manners in wording to signal suitability for upper-/middle-class audiences and to attract respondents of the desired social standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anonymity, initials and intermediaries for replies
rubrics_metrics.description: Many adverts direct replies to initials (e.g., 'T. S., at Mr Sharp's') or to be left at stationers/coffee-houses rather than giving full addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ initials, care-of addresses (stationers, coffee-houses), or third-party collection points to maintain advertiser/respondent privacy and to screen replies; this was a common production convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create urgency or scarcity with limited insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'N.B. — This advertisement will be inserted in this morning's Paper only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting an advertisement's run (or calling out a single-insertion N.B.) is used to create urgency or exclusivity and can pressure quick responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to cupidity with get-rich promises (specious schemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverts promising 'an eligible method of converting hundreds into Thousands, in a few weeks' or a 'Method which reduces it almost to a certainty to obtain a very considerable sum, by insuring of Numbers in the Lottery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such adverts deliberately target those driven by greed; the text implicitly warns these are speculative or potentially fraudulent appeals — a criterion for skepticism when evaluating adverts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of financial leverage / purchase of offices as a social-practice advert
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements offering to 'advance any Nobleman or Gentleman the sum of Three Thousand Pounds ... provided the Mortgager will, thro' his Interest, procure a place in any genteel Department' demonstrate market practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ads openly offering capital in return for influence or office illustrate a historical norm of buying sinecures; when producing/evaluating such adverts, note the explicit transactional framing and promised secrecy.
